You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo energy harvester (sinusoidal current source + Cp + Rp).
    *   Goal: Power a load RL from a storage capacitor at node `out`.
    *   Constraints:
        *   `vavg` >= 1.8 V (S1-S6)
        *   `vmax` <= 3.6 V (S1-S6)
        *   `vpp` <= 0.05 V (S1-S6)
        *   `tup` <= 0.4 s (S1-S6)
        *   `dv` <= 0.02 V (S1-S6)
    *   Operating conditions: S1 (nominal), S2 (heavy load), S3 (strong excitation, light load), S4 (weak excitation), S5 (low frequency), S6 (hot, higher Cp).
    *   Open circuit voltage is low (~3.2 V), so diode drops are significant.

    *   S2 (Heavy load): `vavg` failed (1.76 V < 1.8 V).
    *   S3 (Strong excitation, light load): `vmax` failed (5.72 V > 3.6 V), `vpp` failed (84.4 mV > 50 mV), `dv` failed.
    *   S4 (Weak excitation): `vavg` failed (1.51 V < 1.8 V), `tup` failed.
    *   S5 (Low frequency): `dv` failed.
    *   Conclusion: The full-bridge rectifier (FBR) is too inefficient for weak/heavy loads and lacks voltage regulation for strong excitations.

    *   Standard FBR is passive. To improve efficiency, we need to reduce the voltage drop or implement Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE) or Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI).
    *   *SSH:* Flipping the voltage across Cp at the peaks increases the energy extracted.
    *   *SECE:* Uses a switch and an inductor to extract energy from the piezo capacitance more efficiently.
    *   *Zener Clamping:* Needed to prevent `vmax` from exceeding 3.6 V (S3).
    *   *Storage Capacitor:* Needs to be large enough to minimize ripple (`vpp`) and stabilize `vavg`.

    *   **Topology 1: SSHI-like (Inductive Inversion) + FBR + Zener**
        *   An inductor L and a switch S are used to invert the voltage on the piezo capacitor Cp.
        *   Actually, a simpler approach for low voltage is a "Half-Bridge" or a "Synchronous Rectifier" if we have the controller.
        *   Let's try a classic SSHI topology:
            1. Piezo terminals (pzp, pzn).
            2. L and S in parallel with the piezo to flip polarity at the peaks (sync on "both" edges).
            3. A rectifier to feed the storage capacitor.
            *Wait*, the components allowed are 16. L, S, SYNC, and FBR take several.
            *   L1: `pzp` to `n1`.
            *   S1: `n1` to `pzn`.
            *   SYNC G1: controls S1.
            *   Then a rectifier from the piezo to `out`.

    *   **Topology 2: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)**
        *   Piezo is connected to a switch S1.
        *   S1 connects `pzp` to an LC circuit or directly to the output when the voltage is high.
        *   A more common SECE:
            1. S1 connects `pzp` to an inductor L1.
            2. L1 connects to a diode D1 and then to `out`.
            3. D1 prevents backflow.
            4. S1 closes at the voltage peaks.
            5. The inductor transfers the energy from Cp to Cout.
            6. Zener diode to clamp `out` at 3.3 V.

    *   **Topology 3: FBR + Zener (Improved Reference)**
        *   The reference design failed mostly on efficiency (S2, S4) and overvoltage (S3).
        *   Adding a Zener clamp `DZ33` to `out` fixes S3's `vmax`.
        *   To fix S2/S4, we need more energy. An inductor-based boost or SSHI is necessary.

    *   *Idea 1 (SSHI-based):*
        *   L1 and S1 in parallel with the piezo to flip polarity.
        *   D1-D4 as a full bridge to `out`.
        *   D5 as a Zener clamp `DZ33` on `out`.
        *   Cout on `out`.
        *   This increases the effective voltage available to the bridge.

    *   *Idea 2 (SECE-based):*
        *   Piezo terminals `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   S1 connects `pzp` to `n1`.
        *   S2 connects `pzn` to `n1`.
        *   L1 connects `n1` to `n2`.
        *   D1 (DSCH) connects `n2` to `out`.
        *   Cout on `out`.
        *   D_zener (DZ33) from `0` to `out`.
        *   This is basically a synchronous charge pump.

    *   *Idea 3 (Simple Boost/Charge pump variant):*
        *   A simplified SSHI using only one switch and one inductor to flip the voltage, followed by a rectifier.
        *   L1 from `pzp` to `n1`.
        *   S1 from `n1` to `pzn`.
        *   Rectifier: D1(`pzp`, `out`), D2(`pzn`, `out`), D3(`0`, `pzp`), D4(`0`, `pzn`). (Wait, that's a bridge).
        *   Let's try a simpler bridge: D1(`pzp`, `out`), D2(`pzn`, `out`) is not a bridge.
        *   Full bridge: `pzp`->`out`, `pzn`->`out` (wait, this is wrong), `0`->`pzp`, `0`->`pzn`. No.
        *   Correct Full Bridge:
            D1: `pzp` -> `out`
            D2: `pzn` -> `out` (Wait, this doesn't make sense for a bridge)
            Standard Bridge:
            D1: `pzp` -> `out`
            D2: `pzn` -> `out` (No)
            D1: `pzp` -> `out`
            D2: `0` -> `pzp` (No)
            Let's use the reference bridge: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
            Wait, the reference bridge provided in the prompt is: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`. Let me re-read.
            "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]".
            Wait, if D1 is `pzp`->`out` and D2 is `pzn`->`out`, then both `pzp` and `pzn` are connected to `out`. If D3 is `0`->`pzp` and D4 is `0`->`pzn`, then both are connected to ground. This is a standard bridge:
            When `pzp` > 0 and `pzp` > `out`, D1 conducts. Then `pzn` is negative, so D4 conducts.
            When `pzp` < 0 and `pzn` > `out`, D2 conducts. Then `pzp` is negative, so D3 conducts.
            Yes, this is a standard bridge.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener**
        *   L1: `pzp` to `n1`
        *   S1: `n1` to `pzn`
        *   G1: SYNC (edges: "both", ton: calculated later)
        *   FBR:
            D1: `pzp` to `out`
            D2: `pzn` to `out`
            D3: `0` to `pzp`
            D4: `0` to `pzn`
        *   D_zener: `0` to `out` (DZ33)
        *   C_out: `out` to `0`

    *   **Design 2: SECE (Simplified)**
        *   S1: `pzp` to `n1`
        *   S2: `pzn` to `n1`
        *   L1: `n1` to `n2`
        *   D1: `n2` to `out` (DSCH)
        *   C_out: `out` to `0`
        *   D_zener: `0` to `out` (DZ33)
        *   G1: SYNC (edges: "pos", ctrl S1)
        *   G2: SYNC (edges: "neg", ctrl S2)

    *   **Design 3: Half-Wave Synchronous + Zener**
        *   S1: `pzp` to `n1`
        *   L1: `n1` to `out`
        *   D1: `pzp` to `out` (Wait, no)
        *   Let's try a simpler variant of the SSHI:
            S1: `pzp` to `n1`
            L1: `n1` to `pzn`
            FBR: D1..D4 as above.
            D_zener: `0` to `out`.
            C_out: `out` to `0`.
            This is effectively the same as Design 1. Let's try a different approach for Design 3.

    *   **Design 3 (Alternative): Capacitive Charge Pump / Doubler?**
        *   Piezo voltage is low, so we need to boost.
        *   Maybe a simple buck-boost using the SYNC?
        *   L1: `pzp` to `n1`
        *   S1: `n1` to `0`
        *   D1: `n1` to `out`
        *   C_out: `out` to `0`
        *   D_zener: `0` to `out`
        *   G1: SYNC (edges: "both")
        *   This is a basic boost.

    *   L1 = 10 mH, C_out = 2.2 uF.
    *   D_zener = DZ33.
    *   FBR diodes = DSCH.
    *   S1 controlled by G1 (edges="both", phase=0).

    *   G1 (pos) -> S1, G2 (neg) -> S2.
    *   S1: `pzp` to `n1`, S2: `pzn` to `n1`.
    *   L1: `n1` to `n2`.
    *   D1: `n2` to `out`.
    *   C_out: `out` to `0`.
    *   D_zener: `0` to `out`.

    *   S1: `pzp` to `n1`, L1: `n1` to `0`, D1: `n1` to `out`, C_out: `out` to `0`, D_zener: `0` to `out`.
    *   Wait, this boost is only one-sided.
    *   Let's use a full-bridge synchronous rectifier (S1, S2, S3, S4) if possible, but we only have 4 switches.
    *   A full-bridge synchronous rectifier:
        S1: `pzp` to `out`
        S2: `pzn` to `out`
        S3: `0` to `pzp`
        S4: `0` to `pzn`
        Wait, the SYNC controllers only provide 2.
        If we use G1 for S1 and S3, and G2 for S2 and S4?
        G1 (pos): S1 closes (`pzp` to `out`), S4 closes (`0` to `pzn`).
        G2 (neg): S2 closes (`pzn` to `out`), S3 closes (`0` to `pzp`).
        This replaces the diodes with switches, reducing the drop.
        Combined with a Zener and a large Cout.

    *   Design 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener (Energy increase via voltage flipping)
    *   Design 2: SECE (Energy extraction via inductor)
    *   Design 3: Synchronous FBR + Zener (Efficiency increase via low-drop switches)

    *Let's refine Design 1 (SSHI + FBR + Zener):*
    L1: `pzp` to `n1`, S1: `n1` to `pzn`, G1: `both`, FBR: D1(`pzp`, `out`), D2(`pzn`, `out`), D3(`0`, `pzp`), D4(`0`, `pzn`), D_zener: `0`, `out`, C_out: `out`, `0`.

    *Let's refine Design 2 (SECE):*
    S1: `pzp` to `n1`, S2: `pzn` to `n1`, L1: `n1` to `n2`, D1: `n2` to `out`, D_zener: `0`, `out`, C_out: `out`, `0`.
    G1: `pos` (S1), G2: `neg` (S2).

    *Let's refine Design 3 (Synchronous FBR + Zener):*
    S1: `pzp` to `out`, S4: `0` to `pzn` (ctrl G1, pos)
    S2: `pzn` to `out`, S3: `0` to `pzp` (ctrl G2, neg)
    Wait, one SYNC can only control one switch? "S switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC".
    It doesn't say a SYNC can only control one switch. Let's assume it can control multiple. If not, I'll use 4 switches and 2 SYNCs, but I can't assign one SYNC to two switches unless the syntax allows it. Let's re-read: "`ctrl`: id of a SYNC". This implies a switch has one controller. It doesn't say a SYNC can't be the controller for multiple switches.
    *Wait*, if I can't use one SYNC for two switches, I can't do the synchronous bridge. Let's check the components again: "S switch... (at most 4)", "SYNC ideal synchronous controller... (at most 2)".
    If I have 2 SYNCs, I can control 4 switches only if each SYNC can be assigned to multiple switches. If each SYNC can only control one switch, I'm limited to 2 switches.
    Let's assume 1 SYNC can control multiple switches.

    Actually, a simpler Design 3: FBR + Zener (Reference but with DZ33 and larger C). But the reference already failed `vavg` on S2/S4. So the Synchronous FBR is better.

    Let's double-check the SSHI and SECE.
    SSHI:
    - Piezo is source.
    - Inductor and switch flip the voltage.
    - Rectifier harvests it.
    SECE:
    - Piezo is source.
    - Switch and inductor extract charge.
    - Diode directs it to storage.

    *Design 1 (SSHI):*
    - Components: L1, S1, G1, D1, D2, D3, D4, D5(zener), C1. (9 components)
    *Design 2 (SECE):*
    - Components: S1, S2, G1, G2, L1, D1, D5(zener), C1. (8 components)
    *Design 3 (Sync FBR):*
    - Components: S1, S2, S3, S4, G1, G2, D5(zener), C1. (8 components)

    Let's verify Design 2 (SECE) connectivity again:
    - Pzp -> S1 -> n1
    - Pzn -> S2 -> n1
    - n1 -> L1 -> n2
    - n2 -> D1 -> out
    - out -> C1 -> 0
    - out -> D_zener(cathode) -> 0 (DZ33)
    - G1 (pos) controls S1, G2 (neg) controls S2.
    Wait, if S1 closes at the positive peak, the charge in Cp flows through L1 and D1 into Cout. This is the standard SECE mechanism.

    Let's verify Design 1 (SSHI) connectivity again:
    - Pzp -> L1 -> n1
    - n1 -> S1 -> Pzn
    - G1 (both) controls S1.
    - Pzp -> D1 -> out
    - Pzn -> D2 -> out
    - 0 -> D3 -> Pzp
    - 0 -> D4 -> Pzn
    - out -> C1 -> 0
    - out -> D_zener(cathode) -> 0 (DZ33)

    Let's verify Design 3 (Sync Bridge) connectivity:
    - Pzp -> S1 -> out (G1, pos)
    - 0 -> S4 -> Pzn (G1, pos)
    - Pzn -> S2 -> out (G2, neg)
    - 0 -> S3 -> Pzp (G2, neg)
    - out -> C1 -> 0
    - out -> D_zener(cathode) -> 0 (DZ33)

    Comparing them:
    - SSHI: High energy gain, but bridge drop still exists.
    - SECE: High efficiency, simple, but needs precise L and ton.
    - Sync Bridge: Lowest drop, but no energy gain (no L).

    S2 and S4 failed on `vavg`, meaning we need *more* energy, not just lower drops. SSHI and SECE provide more energy by exploiting the piezo's capacitance. Sync Bridge only reduces loss.
    Therefore, SSHI and SECE are more promising for S2/S4.

    *Final Polish on Design 1 (SSHI):*
    S1: n1 to pzn, G1: both, L1: pzp to n1.
    Rectifier: D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn).
    Clamp: D5(0, out, DZ33).
    Cap: C1(out, 0).

    *Final Polish on Design 2 (SECE):*
    S1: pzp to n1, G1: pos.
    S2: pzn to n1, G2: neg.
    L1: n1 to n2.
    D1: n2 to out.
    Clamp: D5(0, out, DZ33).
    Cap: C1(out, 0).

    *Final Polish on Design 3 (Modified FBR):*
    Let's try a "Charge Pump" with a SYNC.
    S1: pzp to n1, G1: pos.
    C1: n1 to 0.
    D1: n1 to out.
    Wait, that's just a switch-capacitor pump.
    Let's go with the Synchronous Bridge for diversity, even if it might not solve S2/S4 as well as SSHI/SECE. Actually, a better Design 3 would be a "half-bridge" SSHI or something. Let's stick with the Sync Bridge and see.

    Wait, one more check: "vpp <= 0.05 V". This is very strict. We need a large C_out.
    "tup <= 0.4 s". We need efficient startup.

    Let's refine the SYNC `ton` for SSHI and SECE.
    For SSHI, $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    $C_p = 25$ nF, $L = 10$ mH $\implies t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 3.14 \times 5 \times 10^{-4} \approx 1.5$ ms.
    Wait, the `ton` limit is $1 \mu\text{s}$ ($1e-06$ is not $0.001$, $0.001$ is $1\text{ms}$).
    The limit is `1e-07..0.001`. So $1\text{ms}$ is the maximum.
    If $t_{on} = 1\text{ms}$, $L$ should be around $10\text{mH}$ for $C_p=25\text{nF}$.

    One detail on the full bridge:
    Reference says: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
    Wait, this is:
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: pzn -> out
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    Let's trace:
    If pzp = +V, pzn = -V: D1 conducts (pzp -> out), D4 conducts (0 -> pzn). Correct.
    If pzp = -V, pzn = +V: D2 conducts (pzn -> out), D3 conducts (0 -> pzp). Correct.

    Let's make sure the components are within limits.
    Max components: 16.
    Design 1: 9. Design 2: 8. Design 3: 8. All good.

    *One last check on Design 2 (SECE):*
    S1 (pzp, n1), S2 (pzn, n1), L1 (n1, n2), D1 (n2, out), D5 (0, out), C1 (out, 0).
    G1 (pos) controls S1. G2 (neg) controls S2.
    When S1 closes, current flows from pzp (at peak) through L1 to out.
    Wait, if S1 closes at the positive peak, the voltage at pzp is high. L1 will charge and then discharge into Cout.
    But for SECE to work, we need the energy to be *extracted* from Cp.
    The SECE circuit usually has the inductor and diode in series with the output.
    Yes: `pzp -> S1 -> L1 -> D1 -> out`. This is exactly what I have.
